input.description: That tool's input — same shape you'd pass when calling it directly. For computer items whose action is left_click, right_click, double_click, triple_click, left_click_drag, key or type, and for form_input items, include action_summary in the item's input, as you would when calling that tool directly.

actions.description: List of tool calls to execute sequentially. Example: [{"name":"computer","input":{"action":"left_click","ref":"ref_12"}},{"name":"computer","input":{"action":"type","text":"hello"}},{"name":"computer","input":{"action":"screenshot"}}]

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__computer
tools.description: Mouse/keyboard automation in the Browser pane. Clicks accept either `coordinate` (pixels in the coordinate frame of the most recent `computer{action:"screenshot"}` — reported with every scaled screenshot; equal to the image's pixels for unscaled ones) or `ref` (a `ref_N` from read_page/find). Whenever you intend to click on an element like an icon, you should consult a screenshot to determine the coordinates of the element first; after the tab loads a different site, take a new screenshot before clicking by `coordinate`.

schema.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__computer
schema.description: Mouse/keyboard automation in the Browser pane. Clicks accept either `coordinate` (pixels in the coordinate frame of the most recent `computer{action:"screenshot"}` — reported with every scaled screenshot; equal to the image's pixels for unscaled ones) or `ref` (a `ref_N` from read_page/find). Whenever you intend to click on an element like an icon, you should consult a screenshot to determine the coordinates of the element first; after the tab loads a different site, take a new screenshot before clicking by `coordinate`.

tabId.description: Tab to act on within the preview context. Omit for the fronted tab; get ids from tabs_context.

action.description:
The action to perform:
* `left_click`: Click the left mouse button at the specified coordinates.
* `right_click`: Click the right mouse button at the specified coordinates to open context menus.
* `double_click`: Double-click the left mouse button at the specified coordinates.
* `triple_click`: Triple-click the left mouse button at the specified coordinates.
* `type`: Type a string of text.
* `screenshot`: Take a screenshot of the screen.
* `wait`: Wait for a specified number of seconds.
* `scroll`: Scroll up, down, left, or right at the specified coordinates.
* `key`: Press a specific keyboard key.
* `left_click_drag`: Drag from start_coordinate to coordinate.
* `zoom`: Take a screenshot of a specific region for closer inspection.
* `scroll_to`: Scroll an element into view using its element reference ID from read_page or find tools.
* `hover`: Move the mouse cursor to the specified coordinates or element without clicking. Useful for revealing tooltips, dropdown menus, or triggering hover states.

coordinate.description: (x, y): The x (pixels from the left edge) and y (pixels from the top edge) coordinates. Required for `left_click`, `right_click`, `double_click`, `triple_click`, and `scroll`. For `left_click_drag`, this is the end position.

text.description: The text to type (for `type` action) or the key(s) to press (for `key` action). For `key` action: Provide space-separated keys (e.g., "Backspace Backspace Delete"). Supports keyboard shortcuts using the platform's modifier key (use "cmd" on Mac, "ctrl" on Windows/Linux, e.g., "cmd+a" or "ctrl+a" for select all). Page zoom shortcuts (e.g. "cmd+=", "ctrl+-", "cmd+0") are not supported - use the `zoom` action to magnify a region of the page instead.

duration.description: The number of seconds to wait. Required for `wait`. Maximum 10 seconds.

scroll_direction.description: The direction to scroll. Required for `scroll`.

scroll_amount.description: The number of scroll wheel ticks. Optional for `scroll`, defaults to 3.

region.description: (x0, y0, x1, y1): The rectangular region to capture for `zoom`. Coordinates define a rectangle from top-left (x0, y0) to bottom-right (x1, y1) in pixels from the viewport origin. Required for `zoom` action. Useful for inspecting small UI elements like icons, buttons, or text.

scale.description: For `screenshot` and `zoom` only. Scale factor in [0.1, 1] for the returned image; 1 (default) uses the full image token budget, 0.5 returns an image at half the width and height (~quarter of the tokens). Coordinates are ALWAYS in the full-resolution coordinate frame (reported with every scaled screenshot), never in the scaled image's own pixels.

repeat.description: Number of times to repeat the key sequence. Only applicable for `key` action. Must be a positive integer between 1 and 100. Default is 1. Useful for navigation tasks like pressing arrow keys multiple times.

ref.description: Element reference ID from read_page or find tools (e.g., "ref_1", "ref_2"). Required for `scroll_to` action. Can be used as alternative to `coordinate` for click actions.

modifiers.description: Modifier keys for click actions. Supports: "ctrl", "shift", "alt", "cmd" (or "meta"), "win" (or "windows"). Can be combined with "+" (e.g., "ctrl+shift", "cmd+alt"). Optional.

action_summary.description: A few words saying what this action does on the page and to what, for example 'Sends the drafted reply to pat@example.com' or 'Opens the Filters menu'. Set it on every left_click, right_click, double_click, triple_click, left_click_drag, key and type action. State the effect only, and accurately: no reasons, nothing about what you were asked or allowed to do, no passwords or other secrets.

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__resize_window
tools.description: Emulate a viewport size in the Browser pane tab. Presets: mobile (375x812), tablet (768x1024), or desktop, which clears the size emulation and returns the tab to the pane's own responsive size. Custom sizes need both width and height. An emulated size applies to that tab across reloads and navigation (scaled down to fit when it is larger than the pane): reset it with preset "desktop" as soon as you finish testing. The desktop app may also clear a size you set when your turn ends, so set it again in a later turn if you still need it. A size the user picked from the pane's own Viewport menu is theirs and stays until they or you change it; leave it unless they ask. colorScheme (light/dark) emulates prefers-color-scheme on that tab; it survives reloads and preset "desktop" does not touch it, but the pane re-syncs the tab to the app's light/dark theme when that theme changes or the pane reopens; local documents and static HTML previews always render light. The mobile preset (and any width < 768) also emulates a mobile device: Android Chrome user agent and 5 touch points, so pages detect a touch phone; your clicks still arrive as mouse clicks. Reload the page after switching so load-time device gates re-run.

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Code_iOS_Simulator__control
tools.description: Run, test, and visually verify iOS apps in the iOS Simulator on this Mac. Use this whenever the user wants to see or try their iOS app — "run my app", "test this on iPhone", "does this look right?", "try the new screen" — not only when they mention the simulator by name. Simulator only: this tool cannot drive or stream a physical iPhone or iPad. If the user wants the app on their real device ("on my iPhone", "on my device"), build and deploy for the device with your normal build tools instead, and say the live panel only shows simulators. 'attach' opens a live panel so the user can watch — when the user wants to see the app, call 'attach' FIRST, before building: it is cheap, opens instantly on a booted simulator, and errors harmlessly when nothing is booted (boot or build, then retry it). 'launch' installs and launches a built .app — build it first, with the user's own build tooling or this server's 'build' tool when this session has it; launch re-attaches on its own, but do not rely on that instead of the early attach. Screenshots and tap/swipe/text verification are headless and need no panel. Don't open the panel when the user only asked to build/compile or to run unit tests. Coordinates are in device points (origin top-left); the 'launch' result reports the device's point dimensions.

Skip it only when the user has no interest in watching; 'launch' installs and launches an .app (it also re-attaches, but call 'attach' early rather than relying on that); 'screenshot' returns a PNG of the current screen; 'tap'/'swipe'/'text'/'button' inject input; 'press_key' presses a hardware key 'count' times: return, delete (backspace), an arrow, select_all, undo or redo (a key also hides the on-screen keyboard); 'set_keyboard' shows or hides the on-screen keyboard (it appears only while a text field has focus, and 'press_key' and 'text' hide it again); 'rotate' turns the device a quarter turn left or right ('direction'); take a 'screenshot' after it and tap in that screenshot's frame, however it comes back; 'touch_path' performs a single-finger drag along an arbitrary path (eased curves, long-press-then-drag); 'touch2_path' is the two-finger variant for pinch/rotate; 'open_url' opens a deep link; 'detach' closes the panel/stream. # Project rules

This is a assignment: a tip and bill splitter that runs in a web browser. I direct the work, review everything and test the app myself. You write the code and help me draft three product documents, in this order: docs/app-roles.md, docs/jobs-to-be-done.md and docs/user-stories.md.

## What good looks like
- A small app that fully works and is well specified beats a big one that doesn't.
- The documents and the README must describe exactly what was built. Never claim something works unless it was verified.
- Every claim in a doc or the README is backed by a passing test, a command that was run, or a check that was done and recorded. If something was not checked, say so plainly.
- A story is Implemented only when every one of its acceptance criteria has passed, by an automated test or by a manual check I confirmed. Otherwise it is Not implemented.

## Technical rules
- Plain HTML, CSS and JavaScript. No build step, no dependencies, no frameworks and no ES modules, so the app opens by double-clicking src/index.html.
- Nothing is loaded from outside: no network requests, no external fonts or libraries.
- Logic lives in plain CommonJS-style files that also load as classic browser scripts and through require() in Node. package.json must not set "type": "module".
- Money is integer cents. Never use floating point for amounts.
- Keep the UI thin. app.js only reads the fields, calls the pure view-model function and writes the result to the page. No money logic and no message text in app.js.
- Every message the user can see lives in one constants file, and the docs quote those exact strings.
- Never show NaN, Infinity, undefined or exponent notation on the page.
- Tests use node:test and run with `node --test` on Node 20 or newer. Test files are named *.test.js, and test names start with the criterion id, such as S-1.1. Keep the tests free of anything newer than Node 20.

## Working rules
- Don't add features, dependencies or files beyond what we agree. Ask before large changes.
- If a criterion in the docs looks wrong or impossible, tell me. Don't change it quietly.
- Don't say something is verified in a browser unless you ran it there. I check browser behavior myself.
- If I edit anything by hand, I'll tell you, and it goes in the README.
- Commit locally after each stage (setup, docs, logic and tests, UI, fixes, test report and README) with a clear message. Never push and never add a remote.
- Keep the assessment and the reviewers out of code comments, UI text and the three product docs. The README can mention that this is a take-home.
- Don't copy the assignment brief into any file in this repository, except the unedited transcript.
- Keep replies short and in plain English, and say what you changed.
- Run `npm test` before you call a stage done, and report the real counts.
- To show that the tests catch bugs, plant one bug at a time in a throwaway copy outside the project, never in the working tree, and say which test failed.
- Leave no placeholders (TODO or bracketed fill-ins) in a committed file. If you need a fact only I have, such as a model name or a browser version, ask me.
- Keep temporary tooling out of the project. If a preview server needs a config file, it goes in the git-ignored .claude/ folder and is deleted afterwards.

[Heading1] Take-Home Assignment: Build a Calculator Web App with an AI Coding Tool
KnowledgeCity, Technology Division
[Heading2] About this assignment
Thank you for your interest in joining KnowledgeCity. Our product software is built with AI coding tools, and the people in product and delivery roles direct that work: they decide who a product is for, define what it must do, and check that what the AI builds is correct. This assignment asks you to do the same on a small scale.
You will build a calculator web application with an AI coding tool and send us three things: the working source code, the transcript of your session with the AI tool, and a short set of product documents. The code shows us the result, the transcript shows us how you got there, and the documents show us how you think about users and requirements.
Plan for about 2 to 4 hours. A small app that works and is well specified is worth more to us than a large one that does not.
[Heading2] The task
Build a calculator that runs in a web browser, using an AI coding tool to write the code.
The kind of calculator is your choice: a basic arithmetic calculator, a scientific calculator, a loan or mortgage calculator, a tip and bill splitter, or anything else that calculates. Deciding who it is for and what problem it solves is part of the assignment, so state your choice and your reasons in the README.
[Heading3] Requirements
* It runs in a current version of Chrome, Edge, Firefox or Safari.
* A reviewer can start it on their own computer by following your README, with no paid accounts, API keys or cloud services. A public URL where the app is already running is welcome in addition to this, not instead of it.
* Any programming language, framework or library is fine.
* Every user story you mark as Implemented works in the running app exactly as its acceptance criteria describe.
* Invalid input and error cases, such as division by zero, produce a clear message, never a crash or a wrong result.
[Heading3] Using an AI coding tool
* Use any AI coding tool: Claude Code, OpenAI Codex, Cursor, GitHub Copilot, Windsurf, Gemini CLI or similar.
* The AI tool writes the code. Your job is to direct it: explain the problem, give it the context it needs, review what it produces, test the result and correct it.
* If you change any code by hand, list those changes in the README.
* You may work across several sessions or several tools. Send the transcript of every session.
* You may use AI to help write the product documents too. You are responsible for their content and should be ready to explain any part of them.
[Heading2] What to submit
[Heading3] Source code
* The complete source code, without installed dependencies or build output (for example, leave out node_modules, virtual environments and dist folders).
* A README file in the root folder that covers: what the app is and who it is for; the prerequisites (for example, Node.js 20); the exact commands to install and start the app; how to run the tests, if you wrote any; which AI tool and model you used; any code you changed by hand; and any assumptions you made.
[Heading3] Session transcript
The transcript is the full record of your conversation with the AI tool: your prompts exactly as you typed them and the tool's responses, from the first message to the last. It shows us how you work with AI, so it matters as much as the code.
* Export it with the tool's own export feature. In Claude Code, the /export command saves the conversation to a file, and session logs are also kept under ~/.claude/projects/. The OpenAI Codex CLI keeps session logs under ~/.codex/sessions/. Other tools usually have an export or copy option on the chat.
* Send the export as it is. A summary of the session, including one the AI tool writes for you at the end, does not count as the transcript.
* Before you send it, remove any passwords, API keys or tokens, and change nothing else.
[Heading3] Product documents
Write three documents, in this order, because each one builds on the one before it.
| Document | Answers | Format of each entry |
| App Roles | Who uses the app | "A [role] is [who this person is and their situation]. They can [what they see and do in the app]. They must never [what the app must prevent]", where the last part applies. |
| Jobs To Be Done | Why they use it | "When [situation], I want to [motivation], so I can [expected outcome]." Each job names the role it belongs to. |
| User Stories with Acceptance Criteria | How the app helps them get the job done | "As a [role], I want [capability], so that [benefit]." Each story names the job it serves and has acceptance criteria and a status. |
* App Roles. A calculator may have one role or several. Either is fine, as long as each role describes a real kind of person and explains how their needs differ from the other roles.
* Jobs To Be Done. A job describes what the person needs to get done whether or not your app exists, so it does not mention your app or its features. If a job cannot be written without naming a button or a screen, it is a feature, not a job.
* User Stories. Every story names the job it serves, and every job names the role it belongs to. A story that serves no job does not belong in the list.
* Acceptance criteria. Write specific, testable statements of how the app behaves, preferably as "Given [starting state], when [action], then [observable result]". Cover the normal case and the cases where things go wrong: invalid input, boundary values, very large or very small numbers, and what happens when the user carries on after a result or an error.
* Status. Mark each story Implemented or Not implemented, based on what the app does today. Stories you would build next are welcome, marked Not implemented.
Markdown, PDF, Word or Google Docs are all fine. Put the files in a docs folder, or link to them from the README.
[Heading3] Example of the format
This example uses a meeting room booking app, so it does not overlap with your calculator.
* App Role. "An Office Employee is a staff member who books rooms for their own meetings. They can see which rooms are free and see their own bookings. They can create and cancel their own bookings. They must never cancel another person's booking."
* Job J-1 (Office Employee). "When I need to meet colleagues in person, I want to secure a suitable space in advance, so I can hold the meeting without searching for a free room on the day."
* User Story S-1 (serves J-1, Implemented). "As an Office Employee, I want to see which rooms are free at a time I choose, so that I can book one without checking each room."
* Given rooms A and B are free from 10:00 to 11:00 and room C is booked, when I search for 10:00 to 11:00, then I see rooms A and B and I do not see room C.
* Given I enter an end time earlier than the start time, when I search, then I see the message "End time must be after the start time" and no rooms are listed.
[Heading2] Packaging and sending
Organize the package like this (the layout of the source folder is up to you):
firstname-lastname-calculator/
  README.md
  src/
  docs/
    app-roles.md
    jobs-to-be-done.md
    user-stories.md
  transcripts/
    session-01.md
* When you receive this assignment, reply to confirm and tell us when you expect to submit.
* Email your submission to the HR contact who sent you this assignment, by the deadline in their email.
* Share the package as a link: a Google Drive folder or a Git repository on GitHub, GitLab or Bitbucket, open to anyone who has the link. Many email systems, Gmail included, block .zip attachments that contain code, so a link is more reliable than an attachment.
* Use the subject line: Take-home assignment: [the role you applied for], [your full name].
* In the email, include the link, the live URL if you deployed the app, the AI tools and models you used, and roughly how long you spent.
[Heading2] How we review your submission
* It works. We follow your README on a clean computer and use the app the way one of your users would. Automated tests are welcome, and we still check the behavior by hand.
* Product thinking. The roles describe real people with different needs, the jobs are free of solutions, every story traces to a job, and the acceptance criteria are testable and cover error and edge cases.
* Working with AI. From the transcript: how you framed the problem, what context you gave the tool, how you checked its output, and which mistakes you caught and fixed.
* Accuracy. The documents and the README describe what was actually built. A story honestly marked Not implemented counts for more than an overstated claim.
* Delivery and communication. You told us when to expect your submission and delivered by then, and the package is clear and easy to review.
Be ready to walk us through your submission and explain your decisions in a follow-up conversation.
[Heading2] Questions
If anything in this assignment is unclear, ask your HR contact. You can also make a reasonable assumption and write it down in the README. How you handle open questions is part of what we look at.

- **"Works exactly as the criteria say"** means exact message text in the criteria. Docs come before code, so strings are fixed in the docs, then copied to the constants file, and they can drift. A fix is one test that every fixed message in the constants file appears word for word in the stories doc. That needs your OK.
- **README "install and start commands".** The app has no install step. The README says so and gives an open-file command per OS. Node is only for tests.
- **Yours, not mine.** The HR reply with a date, and the email (subject, link, tools and models, hours spent). The email names the model: I run as `claude-sonnet-5-5`, so tell me if you switch. A public URL is optional, and CLAUDE.md says never push, so skip it unless you host it by hand.

**In your choice and setup**
- **Floats give wrong cents.** Verified in Node: `(0.3*0.15).toFixed(2)` prints `0.04`, but half-up of 0.045 is 0.05. Integer cents fix it.
- **`type="number"` fields are a trap.** They accept `1e5`, turn bad text into an empty value, and vary by locale. That breaks "no exponent" and "clear message". Use text fields and parse the text ourselves.
- **One actor.** There are no accounts or permissions, so a second role would be invented unless you have a real second person in mind. The brief allows one role.
- **Node.** Only v24.21.0 is installed here (npm 11.19.0, checked). CLAUDE.md says 20 or newer, so the README can only say "run on 24.21.0". A Node 20 run needs a download, and I would ask first.
- **No DOM in Node tests.** There is no jsdom and no dependencies. Page-behaviour criteria, such as live update and the message next to a field, are manual checks you confirm. The rest I test through the view-model. I will not call the page tested.
- **Same author, same blind spot.** I write the code and the tests. Expected values will be hand-computed from the criteria, not from the code's formula. Planted-bug demos cover the rest.

### 3. Suggested v1 scope

**In v1**
- One page with three text fields: bill, tip %, number of people.
- Results update live as you type. There is no Calculate button, so no stale result.
- It shows the tip, the total, and what each person pays.
- An empty field gives a neutral hint. A bad field gives a specific message at that field. Any problem hides the result, so there is never a partial result.
- It opens by double-clicking `src/index.html`. No install, storage or network.
- Files:
  - `src/index.html`, `styles.css`, `messages.js` (all UI text), `calc.js` (money logic), `viewmodel.js` (field text in, everything shown out), `app.js` (thin glue).
  - `tests/*.test.js`, a `package.json` with only a `test` script, and `.gitignore`.
- Docs: 1 role, about 3 jobs, about 6 stories and about 25 criteria. Add 2 to 3 "next" stories marked Not implemented.
- Tests use `node:test` on `calc.js` and `viewmodel.js`. They include shares-sum-to-total checks and a scan of every output for `NaN`, `Infinity`, `undefined` and exponent notation. About 4 planted-bug demos run in a throwaway copy.

**Out on purpose**
- Tax field, tip presets, uneven or itemised or named splits, and a per-person tip breakdown.
- Currency symbols, locales, thousands separators and comma decimals.
- Saved history, sharing, accounts, backend and deploy.
- Reset button, dark mode, translations and automated browser tests.
- Accessibility audit (labelled fields only, not audited).

Where one of these earns a story, it becomes "Not implemented".

**Defaults unless you object:** the tip applies to the amount entered, amounts are currency-neutral with two decimals, English only, system fonts.

**Time estimate** (this is a guess, not measured):

| Stage | Minutes |
|---|---|
| Setup and docs | 60 |
| Logic and tests | 40 |
| UI | 25 |
| Browser checks and fixes | 35 |
| Bug demos, test report, README | 30 |
| Export and final read-through | 20 |

That is about 3 h 30 min, with 30 min spare. If a stage overruns, cut stories to Not implemented, not tests.

### 4. Money rules

- **Stored as integer cents.** Bill text becomes cents by string handling, with no `parseFloat` and no `× 100`. The tip rate is integer tenths of a percent (12.5% is 125). People is an integer.
- **Input format.**
  - Bill: digits, optional `.`, at most 2 decimals.
  - Tip: at most 1 decimal.
  - People: digits only.
  - No commas, signs, inner spaces or exponent. Outer spaces are trimmed.
  - Too many decimals gives a message, never silent rounding.
  - Forms like `.5` and `5.` get decided in the criteria, and you will see them.
- **One rounding step.** The tip rounds half-up to the cent: `tip = floor((bill_cents × tenths + 500) / 1000)`. Example: bill 0.30 at 15% is exactly 0.045, so the tip is 0.05. Verified in Node: the formula gives 5 cents and float `toFixed(2)` gives 0.04. Total = bill + tip, exact.
- **Uneven split.**
  - `base = floor(total / people)` and `r = total mod people`.
  - The first `r` people pay `base + 1` cent and the rest pay `base`, so shares always add to the total exactly.
  - Verified example: 100.00 at 0% over 3 people gives base 3333 cents and r 1. One person pays 33.34 and two pay 33.33.
  - The page shows one line: "each pays X" when `r` is 0, otherwise "r people pay A, the other n−r pay B". People are unnamed, so who pays the extra cent does not matter.
  - I rejected rounding every share up (the group overpays) or down (the group underpays).
- **Tiny totals.** Zero-cent shares are allowed. Total 0.01 over 3 people means one pays 0.01 and two pay 0.00.
- **Output.** Two decimals, digits and one `.` only. No symbol and no thousands separators (`1000000.00`). Built from integers by string handling.

| Field | Allowed | Reason |
|---|---|---|
| Bill | 0.01 to 1000000.00 | A zero bill is pointless and gets a message. The cap rejects typos and keeps integer math far below 2^53 (largest product is 10^8 cents × 1000 = 10^11). |
| Tip % | 0 to 100, one decimal | 0 means no tip. Above 100 is almost always a typo. |
| People | 1 to 100, whole number | 0 is the only divide-by-zero case and gets a message. |

### 5. Questions

1. Who is the app for? I suggest one role: a person eating out with a group who works out what everyone owes when the bill arrives. Do you agree, do you want a different person, or do you want two roles (for example a guest and the person who paid the whole bill)? Two roles means more jobs, stories and criteria to write and test.
2. Do you accept the money rules and limits in section 4, especially that the first few people pay one extra cent when the total does not divide evenly? If not, what should change?
3. Is the v1 scope in section 3 right for your time, including the defaults (live results, currency-neutral amounts, no tax field)? If not, what should change?
4. Which browsers and devices can you test in, for example Chrome, Safari, Firefox, Edge or a phone?
5. What deadline did HR give, and have you already replied to confirm receipt and give your expected submission date?

content:
Thanks, here are my answers. If something differs from what you suggested, go with mine.

1. Who it's for: one role, a person at a restaurant table who pays the check and tells everyone what they owe, splitting equally. A made-up second role would just be padding. The one real "must never" is showing a wrong or stale amount, like shares that don't add up to the total or an old result after an input became invalid. Please don't invent others.

2. Sharing: I'll share a public GitHub repo and push it myself at the end. Local commits are fine and I'd like one after each stage (setup, docs, logic and tests, UI, fixes, test report and README) with a clear message. Never push and never add a remote.

3. Browsers: I'll test by hand in [Chrome and Safari], and the README should list only those.
4. Scope: v1 is just the bill amount, a tip percentage (default 15) and the number of people (default 2). It shows the tip, the total and each person's share live as I type, a line showing how an uneven split is shared, and a reset button. Quick-tip buttons, rounding the total up, splitting by items and adding tax separately are out of v1, but we'll document them as Not implemented.
6. Money: integer cents only, no floating point, with the tip percentage stored as basis points. The tip is rounded half-up to the cent, once, on the whole bill, and calculated on the bill as entered. If the total doesn't divide evenly, the leftover cents go one each to the first people, the result should say so, and the shares have to add up exactly to the total.
7. Limits: bill from 0.01 to 1,000,000.00, tip from 0 to 100 with up to two decimals, people from 1 to 50 (whole numbers). Anything else gets a clear message and no result. A bill of 0.01 split three ways (0.01, 0.00, 0.00) is allowed and shown honestly.
8. Inputs: text fields (inputmode="decimal") that we validate ourselves, because input type=number returns an empty value for invalid text and then we can't tell empty from invalid. Digits plus one optional decimal point, and ".5" and "5." are fine but "." on its own is not. Ignore spaces, tabs and non-breaking spaces at the ends, allow leading zeros ("007" is 7), and reject commas, signs, exponents, letters and digits from other scripts. Allow at most two decimals; if a value has too many decimals and is also out of range (a bill of 0.005, say), the decimals message wins. The number of people must be a whole number ("2.5", "2.0" and "2." are rejected), and that field uses inputmode="numeric". Amounts show two decimals, with no currency symbol and no thousands separators, so what you read is what you can type.
9. Thin UI: one pure function takes the raw input strings and returns everything the page shows (messages, formatted amounts, which fields are in error, the split line, the state after reset), and app.js only reads the fields, calls it and writes the result to the page. That way I can test the messages without a browser. Each message shows under the field that caused it, in an aria-live="polite" box linked to the input, and the Result box is emptied and hidden whenever any entry is invalid, so a message and an old amount never show together. The shares are a numbered list under "Each person pays", the button is called Reset and puts the defaults back, clears every message and moves focus to the Bill field, and the page works at 320 px wide and with the keyboard alone.

10. Tests: I want them to be a real strength, not a small suite. Unit tests per acceptance criterion, invariant tests with a seeded random generator that print the seed when one fails, a test for every on-screen message, and a test that fails if the docs and the code drift apart. Also page-file tests that read index.html, styles.css and app.js as text and check the script order, that nothing is loaded from outside, that app.js holds no message text or money logic, and that every id, label and live box is in place. A SEED environment variable replays a failing seed. All of it runs with a plain `npm test` and nothing to install.

11. Docs vs build: statuses follow the evidence, but acceptance criteria only change if the criterion itself was wrong, and you tell me first. We don't weaken a criterion to make it pass. Criteria that depend on the page itself (live updating, messages appearing and disappearing, Reset, the first open) sit in a manual list in the docs-sync test and need a browser check I confirmed. A story that isn't Implemented gets a one-line status note naming the criteria that have no evidence. When you write criteria, check each one's own numbers against the default of 2 people: the leftover note shows for every total with an odd number of cents, so write "no error message", not "no message", unless the total divides evenly.
12. docs/test-report.md has how to run the tests, the last run with real counts, the browsers tested (name, version, operating system, date, checks, who ran them), one row per criterion (how it was verified, and pass, fail, not confirmed or not built) and a list of what is not covered. Only what is true goes in.
13. The README describes only what exists and works, with no badges and no screenshots. It says which commands were actually run and on which system, and you ask me for the model name instead of guessing it.

Please add the product and technical decisions (everything except the deadline and HR details) to CLAUDE.md under a "Decisions" heading, grouped as Product, Money, Inputs and display, UI, Tests, Docs and status, and README, keeping it short and in plain English, then show me the file. Don't create anything else yet.

### Product
- One role: a person at a restaurant table who pays the check and tells everyone what they owe. The split is equal. Don't invent a second role.

- Not in v1, each documented as a Not implemented story: quick-tip buttons, rounding the total up, splitting by items, adding tax separately.
- I test by hand in Chrome and Safari. The README lists only those two.
- I publish the repo on GitHub (public) and push it myself at the end.

### Money
- Integer cents only, as above. The tip percentage is stored as basis points (15% is 1500).
- The tip is the bill as entered times the percentage, rounded half-up to the cent, once, on the whole bill. The total is the bill plus the tip.
- If the total doesn't divide evenly, the leftover cents go one each to the first people. The result says so. The shares add up exactly to the total.
- Limits: bill 0.01 to 1000000.00, tip 0 to 100 with up to two decimals, people 1 to 50 as whole numbers. Anything else gets a clear message and no result.
- A bill of 0.01 split three ways (0.01, 0.00, 0.00) is allowed and shown honestly.

### Inputs and display
- All three fields are text fields that we validate ourselves. Bill and tip use inputmode="decimal". People uses inputmode="numeric". No input type=number: it returns an empty value for invalid text, so we can't tell empty from invalid.
- Bill and tip: digits plus one optional decimal point, at most two decimals. ".5" and "5." are fine. "." on its own is not.
- People: digits only. "2.5", "2.0" and "2." are rejected.
- All three: leading zeros are fine ("007" is 7). Spaces, tabs and non-breaking spaces at the ends are ignored. Commas, signs, exponents, letters and digits from other scripts are rejected.
- If a value has too many decimals and is also out of range (a bill of 0.005), the decimals message wins.
- Amounts show two decimals, with no currency symbol and no thousands separators, so what you read is what you can type.

### UI
- One pure function takes the raw input strings and returns everything the page shows: messages, formatted amounts, which fields are in error, the split line and the state after Reset. app.js only reads the fields, calls it and writes the result to the page. That way I can test the messages without a browser.
- Each message shows under the field that caused it, in an aria-live="polite" box linked to the input.
- The Result box is emptied and hidden whenever any entry is invalid, so a message and an old amount never show together.
- The shares are a numbered list under "Each person pays".
- The button is called Reset. It puts the defaults back, clears every message and moves focus to the Bill field.
- The page works at 320 px wide and with the keyboard alone.

### Tests
- The tests should be a real strength, not a small suite.
- Unit tests for each acceptance criterion.
- Invariant tests with a seeded random generator. They print the seed when one fails, and the SEED environment variable replays it, as in `SEED=12345 npm test`.
- A test for every on-screen message.
- A test that fails if the docs and the code drift apart.
- Page-file tests read index.html, styles.css and app.js as text. They check the script order, that nothing is loaded from outside, that app.js holds no message text or money logic, and that every id, label and live box is in place.
- All of it runs with a plain `npm test` (which runs `node --test`). Nothing to install.

### Docs and status
- Statuses follow the evidence. A criterion changes only if the criterion itself was wrong, and you tell me first. Never weaken a criterion to make it pass.
- Criteria that depend on the page itself (live updating, messages appearing and disappearing, Reset, the first open) sit in a manual list in the docs-sync test. They need a browser check that I confirmed.
- A story that isn't Implemented gets a one-line status note naming the criteria that have no evidence.
- Check each criterion's own numbers against the default of 2 people. The leftover note shows for every total with an odd number of cents, so write "no error message", not "no message", unless the total divides evenly.
- docs/test-report.md has: how to run the tests; the last run with real counts; the browsers tested (name, version, operating system, date, checks, who ran them); one row per criterion (how it was verified, and pass, fail, not confirmed or not built); and a list of what is not covered. Only what is true goes in.

### README
- It describes only what exists and works.
- No badges and no screenshots.
- It says which commands were actually run, and on which system.
- Ask me for the model name. Don't guess it.

- Keep temporary tooling out of the project. If a preview server needs a config file, it goes in the git-ignored .claude/ folder and is deleted afterwards.

## Decisions

### Product
- One role: a person at a restaurant table who pays the check and tells everyone what they owe. The split is equal. Don't invent a second role.
- The one real "must never" is showing a wrong or stale amount: shares that don't add up to the total, or an old result after an input became invalid. Don't invent others.
- The inputs are the bill amount, the tip percentage (default 15) and the number of people (default 2).
- Live as I type, the app shows the tip, the total, each person's share and a line saying how an uneven split is shared. It has a Reset button.
- Not in v1, each documented as a Not implemented story: quick-tip buttons, rounding the total up, splitting by items, adding tax separately.
- I test by hand in Chrome and Safari. The README lists only those two.
- I publish the repo on GitHub (public) and push it myself at the end.

### Money
- Integer cents only, as above. The tip percentage is stored as basis points (15% is 1500).
- The tip is the bill as entered times the percentage, rounded half-up to the cent, once, on the whole bill. The total is the bill plus the tip.
- If the total doesn't divide evenly, the leftover cents go one each to the first people. The result says so. The shares add up exactly to the total.
- Limits: bill 0.01 to 1000000.00, tip 0 to 100 with up to two decimals, people 1 to 50 as whole numbers. Anything else gets a clear message and no result.
- A bill of 0.01 split three ways (0.01, 0.00, 0.00) is allowed and shown honestly.

### Inputs and display
- All three fields are text fields that we validate ourselves. Bill and tip use inputmode="decimal". People uses inputmode="numeric". No input type=number: it returns an empty value for invalid text, so we can't tell empty from invalid.
- Bill and tip: digits plus one optional decimal point, at most two decimals. ".5" and "5." are fine. "." on its own is not.
- People: digits only. "2.5", "2.0" and "2." are rejected.
- All three: leading zeros are fine ("007" is 7). Spaces, tabs and non-breaking spaces at the ends are ignored. Commas, signs, exponents, letters and digits from other scripts are rejected.
- If a value has too many decimals and is also out of range (a bill of 0.005), the decimals message wins.
- Amounts show two decimals, with no currency symbol and no thousands separators, so what you read is what you can type.

### UI
- One pure function takes the raw input strings and returns everything the page shows: messages, formatted amounts, which fields are in error, the split line and the state after Reset. app.js only reads the fields, calls it and writes the result to the page. That way I can test the messages without a browser.
- Each message shows under the field that caused it, in an aria-live="polite" box linked to the input.
- The Result box is emptied and hidden whenever any entry is invalid, so a message and an old amount never show together.
- The shares are a numbered list under "Each person pays".
- The button is called Reset. It puts the defaults back, clears every message and moves focus to the Bill field.
- The page works at 320 px wide and with the keyboard alone.

### Tests
- The tests should be a real strength, not a small suite.
- Unit tests for each acceptance criterion.
- Invariant tests with a seeded random generator. They print the seed when one fails, and the SEED environment variable replays it, as in `SEED=12345 npm test`.
- A test for every on-screen message.
- A test that fails if the docs and the code drift apart.
- Page-file tests read index.html, styles.css and app.js as text. They check the script order, that nothing is loaded from outside, that app.js holds no message text or money logic, and that every id, label and live box is in place.
- All of it runs with a plain `npm test` (which runs `node --test`). Nothing to install.

### Docs and status
- Statuses follow the evidence. A criterion changes only if the criterion itself was wrong, and you tell me first. Never weaken a criterion to make it pass.
- Criteria that depend on the page itself (live updating, messages appearing and disappearing, Reset, the first open) sit in a manual list in the docs-sync test. They need a browser check that I confirmed.
- A story that isn't Implemented gets a one-line status note naming the criteria that have no evidence.
- Check each criterion's own numbers against the default of 2 people. The leftover note shows for every total with an odd number of cents, so write "no error message", not "no message", unless the total divides evenly.
- docs/test-report.md has: how to run the tests; the last run with real counts; the browsers tested (name, version, operating system, date, checks, who ran them); one row per criterion (how it was verified, and pass, fail, not confirmed or not built); and a list of what is not covered. Only what is true goes in.

### README
- It describes only what exists and works.
- No badges and no screenshots.
- It says which commands were actually run, and on which system.
- Ask me for the model name. Don't guess it.

## What good looks like
- A small app that fully works and is well specified beats a big one that doesn't.
- The documents and the README must describe exactly what was built. Never claim something works unless it was verified.
- Every claim in a doc or the README is backed by a passing test, a command that was run, or a check that was done and recorded. If something was not checked, say so plainly.
- A story is Implemented only when every one of its acceptance criteria has passed, by an automated test or by a manual check I confirmed. Otherwise it is Not implemented.

- Plain HTML, CSS and JavaScript. No build step, no dependencies, no frameworks and no ES modules, so the app opens by double-clicking src/index.html.

- Never show NaN, Infinity, undefined or exponent notation on the page.
- Tests use node:test and run with `node --test` on Node 20 or newer. Test files are named *.test.js, and test names start with the criterion id, such as S-1.1. Keep the tests free of anything newer than Node 20.

- Don't add features, dependencies or files beyond what we agree. Ask before large changes.

- Commit locally after each stage (setup, docs, logic and tests, UI, fixes, test report and README) with a clear message. Never push and never add a remote.

```markdown
# Project rules

This is a assignment: a tip and bill splitter that runs in a web browser. I direct the work, review everything and test the app myself. You write the code and help me draft three product documents, in this order: docs/app-roles.md, docs/jobs-to-be-done.md and docs/user-stories.md.

## What good looks like
- A small app that fully works and is well specified beats a big one that doesn't.
- The documents and the README must describe exactly what was built. Never claim something works unless it was verified.
- Every claim in a doc or the README is backed by a passing test, a command that was run, or a check that was done and recorded. If something was not checked, say so plainly.
- A story is Implemented only when every one of its acceptance criteria has passed, by an automated test or by a manual check I confirmed. Otherwise it is Not implemented.

## Technical rules
- Plain HTML, CSS and JavaScript. No build step, no dependencies, no frameworks and no ES modules, so the app opens by double-clicking src/index.html.
- Nothing is loaded from outside: no network requests, no external fonts or libraries.
- Logic lives in plain CommonJS-style files that also load as classic browser scripts and through require() in Node. package.json must not set "type": "module".
- Money is integer cents. Never use floating point for amounts.
- Keep the UI thin. app.js only reads the fields, calls the pure view-model function and writes the result to the page. No money logic and no message text in app.js.
- Every message the user can see lives in one constants file, and the docs quote those exact strings.
- Never show NaN, Infinity, undefined or exponent notation on the page.
- Tests use node:test and run with `node --test` on Node 20 or newer. Test files are named *.test.js, and test names start with the criterion id, such as S-1.1. Keep the tests free of anything newer than Node 20.

## Working rules
- Don't add features, dependencies or files beyond what we agree. Ask before large changes.
- If a criterion in the docs looks wrong or impossible, tell me. Don't change it quietly.
- Don't say something is verified in a browser unless you ran it there. I check browser behavior myself.
- If I edit anything by hand, I'll tell you, and it goes in the README.
- Commit locally after each stage (setup, docs, logic and tests, UI, fixes, test report and README) with a clear message. Never push and never add a remote.
- Keep the assessment and the reviewers out of code comments, UI text and the three product docs. The README can mention that this is a take-home.
- Don't copy the assignment brief into any file in this repository, except the unedited transcript.
- Keep replies short and in plain English, and say what you changed.
- Run `npm test` before you call a stage done, and report the real counts.
- To show that the tests catch bugs, plant one bug at a time in a throwaway copy outside the project, never in the working tree, and say which test failed.
- Leave no placeholders (TODO or bracketed fill-ins) in a committed file. If you need a fact only I have, such as a model name or a browser version, ask me.
- Keep temporary tooling out of the project. If a preview server needs a config file, it goes in the git-ignored .claude/ folder and is deleted afterwards.

## Decisions

### Product
- One role: a person at a restaurant table who pays the check and tells everyone what they owe. The split is equal. Don't invent a second role.
- The one real "must never" is showing a wrong or stale amount: shares that don't add up to the total, or an old result after an input became invalid. Don't invent others.
- The inputs are the bill amount, the tip percentage (default 15) and the number of people (default 2).
- Live as I type, the app shows the tip, the total, each person's share and a line saying how an uneven split is shared. It has a Reset button.
- Not in v1, each documented as a Not implemented story: quick-tip buttons, rounding the total up, splitting by items, adding tax separately.
- I test by hand in Chrome and Safari. The README lists only those two.
- I publish the repo on GitHub (public) and push it myself at the end.

### Money
- Integer cents only, as above. The tip percentage is stored as basis points (15% is 1500).
- The tip is the bill as entered times the percentage, rounded half-up to the cent, once, on the whole bill. The total is the bill plus the tip.
- If the total doesn't divide evenly, the leftover cents go one each to the first people. The result says so. The shares add up exactly to the total.
- Limits: bill 0.01 to 1000000.00, tip 0 to 100 with up to two decimals, people 1 to 50 as whole numbers. Anything else gets a clear message and no result.
- A bill of 0.01 split three ways (0.01, 0.00, 0.00) is allowed and shown honestly.

### Inputs and display
- All three fields are text fields that we validate ourselves. Bill and tip use inputmode="decimal". People uses inputmode="numeric". No input type=number: it returns an empty value for invalid text, so we can't tell empty from invalid.
- Bill and tip: digits plus one optional decimal point, at most two decimals. ".5" and "5." are fine. "." on its own is not.
- People: digits only. "2.5", "2.0" and "2." are rejected.
- All three: leading zeros are fine ("007" is 7). Spaces, tabs and non-breaking spaces at the ends are ignored. Commas, signs, exponents, letters and digits from other scripts are rejected.
- If a value has too many decimals and is also out of range (a bill of 0.005), the decimals message wins.
- Amounts show two decimals, with no currency symbol and no thousands separators, so what you read is what you can type.

### UI
- One pure function takes the raw input strings and returns everything the page shows: messages, formatted amounts, which fields are in error, the split line and the state after Reset. app.js only reads the fields, calls it and writes the result to the page. That way I can test the messages without a browser.
- Each message shows under the field that caused it, in an aria-live="polite" box linked to the input.
- The Result box is emptied and hidden whenever any entry is invalid, so a message and an old amount never show together.
- The shares are a numbered list under "Each person pays".
- The button is called Reset. It puts the defaults back, clears every message and moves focus to the Bill field.
- The page works at 320 px wide and with the keyboard alone.

### Tests
- The tests should be a real strength, not a small suite.
- Unit tests for each acceptance criterion.
- Invariant tests with a seeded random generator. They print the seed when one fails, and the SEED environment variable replays it, as in `SEED=12345 npm test`.
- A test for every on-screen message.
- A test that fails if the docs and the code drift apart.
- Page-file tests read index.html, styles.css and app.js as text. They check the script order, that nothing is loaded from outside, that app.js holds no message text or money logic, and that every id, label and live box is in place.
- All of it runs with a plain `npm test` (which runs `node --test`). Nothing to install.

### Docs and status
- Statuses follow the evidence. A criterion changes only if the criterion itself was wrong, and you tell me first. Never weaken a criterion to make it pass.
- Criteria that depend on the page itself (live updating, messages appearing and disappearing, Reset, the first open) sit in a manual list in the docs-sync test. They need a browser check that I confirmed.
- A story that isn't Implemented gets a one-line status note naming the criteria that have no evidence.
- Check each criterion's own numbers against the default of 2 people. The leftover note shows for every total with an odd number of cents, so write "no error message", not "no message", unless the total divides evenly.
- docs/test-report.md has: how to run the tests; the last run with real counts; the browsers tested (name, version, operating system, date, checks, who ran them); one row per criterion (how it was verified, and pass, fail, not confirmed or not built); and a list of what is not covered. Only what is true goes in.

### README
- It describes only what exists and works.
- No badges and no screenshots.
- It says which commands were actually run, and on which system.
- Ask me for the model name. Don't guess it.
```

# Project rules

This is a take-home assignment for a Product Engineering role: a tip and bill splitter that runs in a web browser. I direct the work, review everything and test the app myself. You write the code and help me draft three product documents, in this order: docs/app-roles.md, docs/jobs-to-be-done.md and docs/user-stories.md.

## What good looks like
- A small app that fully works and is well specified beats a big one that doesn't.
- The documents and the README must describe exactly what was built. Never claim something works unless it was verified.
- Every claim in a doc or the README is backed by a passing test, a command that was run, or a check that was done and recorded. If something was not checked, say so plainly.
- A story is Implemented only when every one of its acceptance criteria has passed, by an automated test or by a manual check I confirmed. Otherwise it is Not implemented.

## Technical rules
- Plain HTML, CSS and JavaScript. No build step, no dependencies, no frameworks and no ES modules, so the app opens by double-clicking src/index.html.
- Nothing is loaded from outside: no network requests, no external fonts or libraries.
- Logic lives in plain CommonJS-style files that also load as classic browser scripts and through require() in Node. package.json must not set "type": "module".
- Money is integer cents. Never use floating point for amounts.
- Keep the UI thin. app.js only reads the fields, calls the pure view-model function and writes the result to the page. No money logic and no message text in app.js.
- Every message the user can see lives in one constants file, and the docs quote those exact strings.
- Never show NaN, Infinity, undefined or exponent notation on the page.
- Tests use node:test and run with `node --test` on Node 20 or newer. Test files are named *.test.js, and test names start with the criterion id, such as S-1.1. Keep the tests free of anything newer than Node 20.

## Working rules
- Don't add features, dependencies or files beyond what we agree. Ask before large changes.
- If a criterion in the docs looks wrong or impossible, tell me. Don't change it quietly.
- Don't say something is verified in a browser unless you ran it there. I check browser behavior myself.
- If I edit anything by hand, I'll tell you, and it goes in the README.
- Commit locally after each stage (setup, docs, logic and tests, UI, fixes, test report and README) with a clear message. Never push and never add a remote.
- Keep the assessment and the reviewers out of code comments, UI text and the three product docs. The README can mention that this is a take-home.
- Don't copy the assignment brief into any file in this repository, except the unedited transcript.
- Keep replies short and in plain English, and say what you changed.
- Run `npm test` before you call a stage done, and report the real counts.
- To show that the tests catch bugs, plant one bug at a time in a throwaway copy outside the project, never in the working tree, and say which test failed.
- Leave no placeholders (TODO or bracketed fill-ins) in a committed file. If you need a fact only I have, such as a model name or a browser version, ask me.
- Keep temporary tooling out of the project. If a preview server needs a config file, it goes in the git-ignored .claude/ folder and is deleted afterwards.

## Decisions

### Product
- One role: a person at a restaurant table who pays the check and tells everyone what they owe. The split is equal. Don't invent a second role.
- The one real "must never" is showing a wrong or stale amount: shares that don't add up to the total, or an old result after an input became invalid. Don't invent others.
- The inputs are the bill amount, the tip percentage (default 15) and the number of people (default 2).
- Live as I type, the app shows the tip, the total, each person's share and a line saying how an uneven split is shared. It has a Reset button.
- Not in v1, each documented as a Not implemented story: quick-tip buttons, rounding the total up, splitting by items, adding tax separately.
- I test by hand in Chrome and Safari. The README and the test report list only the browsers I actually tested, with their versions.
- I publish the repo on GitHub (public) and push it myself at the end.

### Money
- Integer cents only, as above. The tip percentage is stored as basis points (15% is 1500).
- The tip is the bill as entered times the percentage, rounded half-up to the cent, once, on the whole bill. The total is the bill plus the tip.
- If the total doesn't divide evenly, the leftover cents go one each to the first people. The result says so. The shares add up exactly to the total.
- Limits: bill 0.01 to 1000000.00, tip 0 to 100 with up to two decimals, people 1 to 50 as whole numbers. Anything else gets a clear message and no result.
- A bill of 0.01 split three ways (0.01, 0.00, 0.00) is allowed and shown honestly.

### Inputs and display
- All three fields are text fields that we validate ourselves. Bill and tip use inputmode="decimal". People uses inputmode="numeric". No input type=number: it returns an empty value for invalid text, so we can't tell empty from invalid.
- Bill and tip: digits plus one optional decimal point, at most two decimals. ".5" and "5." are fine. "." on its own is not.
- People: digits only. "2.5", "2.0" and "2." are rejected.
- All three: leading zeros are fine ("007" is 7). Spaces, tabs and non-breaking spaces at the ends are ignored. Commas, signs, exponents, letters and digits from other scripts are rejected.
- If a value has too many decimals and is also out of range (a bill of 0.005), the decimals message wins.
- Amounts show two decimals, with no currency symbol and no thousands separators, so what you read is what you can type.

### UI
- One pure function takes the raw input strings and returns everything the page shows: messages, formatted amounts, which fields are in error, the split line and the state after Reset. app.js only reads the fields, calls it and writes the result to the page. That way I can test the messages without a browser.
- Each message shows under the field that caused it, in an aria-live="polite" box linked to the input.
- The Result box is emptied and hidden whenever any entry is invalid, so a message and an old amount never show together.
- The shares are a numbered list under "Each person pays".
- The button is called Reset. It puts the defaults back, clears every message and moves focus to the Bill field.
- The page works at 320 px wide and with the keyboard alone.

### Tests
- The tests should be a real strength, not a small suite.
- Unit tests for each acceptance criterion.
- Invariant tests with a seeded random generator. They print the seed when one fails, and the SEED environment variable replays it, as in `SEED=12345 npm test`.
- A test for every on-screen message.
- A test that fails if the docs and the code drift apart.
- Page-file tests read index.html, styles.css and app.js as text. They check the script order, that nothing is loaded from outside, that app.js holds no message text or money logic, and that every id, label and live box is in place.
- All of it runs with a plain `npm test` (which runs `node --test`). Nothing to install.

### Docs and status
- Statuses follow the evidence. A criterion changes only if the criterion itself was wrong, and you tell me first. Never weaken a criterion to make it pass.
- Criteria that depend on the page itself (live updating, messages appearing and disappearing, Reset, the first open) sit in a manual list in the docs-sync test. They need a browser check that I confirmed.
- A story that isn't Implemented gets a one-line status note naming the criteria that have no evidence.
- Check each criterion's own numbers against the default of 2 people. The leftover note shows for every total with an odd number of cents, so write "no error message", not "no message", unless the total divides evenly.
- docs/test-report.md has: how to run the tests; the last run with real counts; the browsers tested (name, version, operating system, date, checks, who ran them); one row per criterion (how it was verified, and pass, fail, not confirmed or not built); and a list of what is not covered. Only what is true goes in.

### README
- It describes only what exists and works.
- No badges and no screenshots.
- It says which commands were actually run, and on which system.
- Ask me for the model name. Don't guess it.

# Project rules

This is a take-home assignment for a Product Engineering role: a tip and bill splitter that runs in a web browser. I direct the work, review everything and test the app myself. You write the code and help me draft three product documents, in this order: docs/app-roles.md, docs/jobs-to-be-done.md and docs/user-stories.md.

## What good looks like
- A small app that fully works and is well specified beats a big one that doesn't.
- The documents and the README must describe exactly what was built. Never claim something works unless it was verified.
- Every claim in a doc or the README is backed by a passing test, a command that was run, or a check that was done and recorded. If something was not checked, say so plainly.
- A story is Implemented only when every one of its acceptance criteria has passed, by an automated test or by a manual check I confirmed. Otherwise it is Not implemented.

## Technical rules
- Plain HTML, CSS and JavaScript. No build step, no dependencies, no frameworks and no ES modules, so the app opens by double-clicking src/index.html.
- Nothing is loaded from outside: no network requests, no external fonts or libraries.
- Logic lives in plain CommonJS-style files that also load as classic browser scripts and through require() in Node. package.json must not set "type": "module".
- Money is integer cents. Never use floating point for amounts.
- Keep the UI thin. app.js only reads the fields, calls the pure view-model function and writes the result to the page. No money logic and no message text in app.js.
- Every message the user can see lives in one constants file, and the docs quote those exact strings.
- Never show NaN, Infinity, undefined or exponent notation on the page.
- Tests use node:test and run with `node --test` on Node 20 or newer. Test files are named *.test.js, and test names start with the criterion id, such as S-1.1. Tests that guard the docs or the page files start with DOCS- or PAGE- instead of a criterion id. Keep the tests free of anything newer than Node 20.

## Working rules
- Don't add features, dependencies or files beyond what we agree. Ask before large changes.
- If a criterion in the docs looks wrong or impossible, tell me. Don't change it quietly.
- Don't say something is verified in a browser unless you ran it there. I check browser behavior myself.
- If I edit anything by hand, I'll tell you, and it goes in the README.
- Commit locally after each stage (setup, docs, logic and tests, UI, fixes, test report and README) with a clear message. Never push and never add a remote.
- Keep the assessment and the reviewers out of code comments, UI text and the three product docs. The README can mention that this is a take-home.
- Don't copy the assignment brief into any file in this repository, except the unedited transcript.
- Keep replies short and in plain English, and say what you changed.
- Run `npm test` before you call a stage done, and report the real counts.
- To show that the tests catch bugs, plant one bug at a time in a throwaway copy outside the project, never in the working tree, and say which test failed.
- Leave no placeholders (TODO or bracketed fill-ins) in a committed file. If you need a fact only I have, such as a model name or a browser version, ask me.
- Keep temporary tooling out of the project. If a preview server needs a config file, it goes in the git-ignored .claude/ folder and is deleted afterwards.

## Decisions

### Product
- One role: a person at a restaurant table who pays the check and tells everyone what they owe. The split is equal. Don't invent a second role.
- The one real "must never" is showing a wrong or stale amount: shares that don't add up to the total, or an old result after an input became invalid. Don't invent others.
- The inputs are the bill amount, the tip percentage (default 15) and the number of people (default 2).
- Live as I type, the app shows the tip, the total, each person's share and a line saying how an uneven split is shared. It has a Reset button.
- Not in v1: quick-tip buttons, rounding the total up, splitting by items, adding tax separately. Two of them, which we choose when we write the stories, are documented as Not implemented stories. The others are listed as out of scope.
- I test by hand in Chrome and Safari. The README and the test report list only the browsers I actually tested, with their versions.
- I publish the repo on GitHub (public) and push it myself at the end.

### Money
- Integer cents only, as above. The tip percentage is stored as basis points (15% is 1500).
- The tip is the bill as entered times the percentage, rounded half-up to the cent, once, on the whole bill. The total is the bill plus the tip.
- If the total doesn't divide evenly, the leftover cents go one each to the first people. The result says so. The shares add up exactly to the total.
- Limits: bill 0.01 to 1000000.00, tip 0 to 100 with up to two decimals, people 1 to 50 as whole numbers. Anything else gets a clear message and no result.
- A bill of 0.01 split three ways (0.01, 0.00, 0.00) is allowed and shown honestly.

### Inputs and display
- All three fields are text fields that we validate ourselves. Bill and tip use inputmode="decimal". People uses inputmode="numeric". No input type=number: it returns an empty value for invalid text, so we can't tell empty from invalid.
- Bill and tip: digits plus one optional decimal point, at most two decimals. ".5" and "5." are fine. "." on its own is not.
- People: digits only. "2.5", "2.0" and "2." are rejected.
- All three: leading zeros are fine ("007" is 7). Spaces, tabs and non-breaking spaces at the ends are ignored. Commas, signs, exponents, letters and digits from other scripts are rejected.
- If a value has too many decimals and is also out of range (a bill of 0.005), the decimals message wins.
- An empty bill is never an error: there is just no result yet. That covers the first open, the state after Reset, and a bill I delete. An empty tip field or an empty people field is an error with its own message.
- Amounts show two decimals, with no currency symbol and no thousands separators, so what you read is what you can type.

### UI
- One pure function takes the raw input strings and returns everything the page shows: messages, formatted amounts, which fields are in error, the split line and the state after Reset. app.js only reads the fields, calls it and writes the result to the page. That way I can test the messages without a browser.
- Static labels (field names, button text, headings) are not messages and stay in index.html. The every-message rule covers only text the app produces at run time, such as errors, results and the split line.
- Each message shows under the field that caused it, in an aria-live="polite" box linked to the input.
- The Result box is emptied and hidden whenever any entry is invalid, so a message and an old amount never show together.
- The shares are a numbered list under "Each person pays".
- The button is called Reset. It puts the defaults back, clears every message and moves focus to the Bill field.
- The page works at 320 px wide and with the keyboard alone.

### Tests
- The tests should be a real strength, not a small suite.
- Unit tests for each acceptance criterion.
- Invariant tests with a seeded random generator. They print the seed when one fails, and the SEED environment variable replays it, as in `SEED=12345 npm test`.
- A test for every on-screen message.
- A test that fails if the docs and the code drift apart.
- Page-file tests read index.html, styles.css and app.js as text. They check the script order, that nothing is loaded from outside, that app.js holds no message text or money logic, and that every id, label and live box is in place.
- All of it runs with a plain `npm test` (which runs `node --test`). Nothing to install.

### Docs and status
- Statuses follow the evidence. A criterion changes only if the criterion itself was wrong, and you tell me first. Never weaken a criterion to make it pass.
- Criteria that depend on the page itself (live updating, messages appearing and disappearing, Reset, the first open) sit in a manual list in the docs-sync test. They need a browser check that I confirmed.
- A page-dependent criterion counts as passed only when I confirmed it in every browser the README lists. The README lists only browsers I actually tested.
- A story that isn't Implemented gets a one-line status note naming the criteria that have no evidence.
- Check each criterion's own numbers against the default of 2 people. The leftover note shows for every total with an odd number of cents, so write "no error message", not "no message", unless the total divides evenly.
- docs/test-report.md has: how to run the tests; the last run with real counts; the browsers tested (name, version, operating system, date, checks, who ran them); one row per criterion (how it was verified, and pass, fail, not confirmed or not built); and a list of what is not covered. Only what is true goes in.

### README
- It describes only what exists and works.
- No badges and no screenshots.
- It says which commands were actually run, and on which system.
- Ask me for the model name. Don't guess it.

# App Roles

## Table Payer

A Table Payer is a person having a meal at a restaurant with friends, family or coworkers, anywhere from two people to a large table. The group has agreed to split the bill equally, and this person settles it with the restaurant, so they pay the whole amount and then have to collect each person's share. They want to add a fair tip and tell everyone exactly what they owe, quickly, while the table waits, without doing sums by hand or arguing over odd cents. What they collect has to add up to what they paid, bill and tip together, because any shortfall comes out of their own pocket. They can enter the bill, a tip percentage and the number of people; see the tip, the total (bill plus tip) and each person's share as they type; see how any leftover cents are shared when the total does not divide evenly; get a clear message when something they entered cannot be used; and start again for the next bill. They must never be shown a wrong or out-of-date amount: shares that do not add up exactly to the total, or an earlier result that is still showing after what they entered has changed or stopped being usable.

## Table Payer

A Table Payer is a person having a meal at a restaurant with friends, family or coworkers, anywhere from two people to a large table. The group has agreed to split the bill equally, and this person settles it with the restaurant, so they pay the whole amount and then have to collect each person's share. They want to add a fair tip and tell everyone exactly what they owe, quickly, while the table waits, without doing sums by hand or arguing over odd cents. What they collect has to add up to what they paid, bill and tip together, because any shortfall comes out of their own pocket. They can enter the bill, a tip percentage and the number of people; see the tip, the total (bill plus tip) and each person's share as they type; see how any leftover cents are shared when the total does not divide evenly; get a clear message when something they entered cannot be used; and start again for the next bill. They must never be shown a wrong or out-of-date amount: shares that do not add up exactly to the total, or an earlier result that is still showing after what they entered has changed or stopped being usable.

input.content:
# Jobs To Be Done

## J-1 (Table Payer): Tell everyone what they owe

When the bill arrives and my table has agreed to split it equally, I want to know exactly what each person owes, tip included, so I can ask each of them for the right amount straight away and settle up.

## J-2 (Table Payer): Settle on a tip

When the table is deciding how much to tip, I want to find out what each tip we are considering would come to in actual money, so I can agree on one that feels fair without guessing.

## J-3 (Table Payer): Share out the odd cents

When the amount we have to pay cannot be divided into equal amounts of whole cents, I want to know exactly how the extra cents are shared out, so I can collect exactly what I paid, with no arguments about odd cents and no shortfall for me to cover.

## J-4 (Table Payer): Redo the sums when things change

When something changes (the table changes its mind, someone joins or leaves, or I find I used a wrong figure) or another bill needs splitting, I want to redo the sums from the corrected figures or from scratch, so I can be sure nothing I tell anyone is based on a wrong or out-of-date figure.

# Jobs To Be Done

When the table is deciding how much to tip, I want to find out what each tip we are considering would come to in actual money, so I can agree on one that feels fair without guessing.

When the amount we have to pay cannot be divided into equal amounts of whole cents, I want to know exactly how the extra cents are shared out, so I can collect exactly what I paid, with no arguments about odd cents and no shortfall for me to cover.

## J-4 (Table Payer): Redo the sums when things change

When something changes (the table changes its mind, someone joins or leaves, or I find I used a wrong figure) or another bill needs splitting, I want to redo the sums from the corrected figures or from scratch, so I can be sure nothing I tell anyone is based on a wrong or out-of-date figure.

```markdown
# Jobs To Be Done

## J-1 (Table Payer): Tell everyone what they owe

When the bill arrives and my table has agreed to split it equally, I want to know exactly what each person owes, tip included, so I can ask each of them for the right amount straight away and settle up.

## J-2 (Table Payer): Settle on a tip

When the table is deciding how much to tip, I want to find out what each tip we are considering would come to in actual money, so I can agree on one that feels fair without guessing.

## J-3 (Table Payer): Share out the odd cents

When the amount we have to pay cannot be divided into equal amounts of whole cents, I want to know exactly how the extra cents are shared out, so I can collect exactly what I paid, with no arguments about odd cents and no shortfall for me to cover.

## J-4 (Table Payer): Redo the sums when things change

When something changes (the table changes its mind, someone joins or leaves, or I find I used a wrong figure) or another bill needs splitting, I want to redo the sums from the corrected figures or from scratch, so I can be sure nothing I tell anyone is based on a wrong or out-of-date figure.

## J-5 (Table Payer): Pay in cash without waiting for change

When I am paying the bill in cash, I want to hand over an amount I can make up from the notes and coins I have on me, so I can pay straight away without waiting for change.
```
